picked.t: Man killed in HCMC after falling tree branch crushes motorbike during thunderstorm
picked.body: Le Van Dung and his wife, 57-year-old Duong Thi Thoan, were heading home from work along An Duong Vuong Street at around 6:30 p.m. when the tragedy struck. As they passed the Ho Chi Minh City University of Education in Cho Quan Ward, a massive tree branch broke in the strong winds and heavy rain , striking their vehicle and throwing them onto the road. The fallen branch, measuring approximately 30 cm in diameter, brought down a canopy large enough to completely block one traffic lane. The couple was transported to An Binh Hospital, about 1.2 km from the scene. Dung succumbed to his severe injuries shortly after arrival. Cho Quan Ward Chairman Nguyen Vo Xuan Ky confirmed that the wife sustained spinal trauma alongside multiple other injuries. She was later transferred to Cho Ray Hospital for treatment. Local authorities have visited the hospital to offer support to her and her family, he said, adding that the ward will formally request the local tree management agency to urgently inspect the area's canopy to prevent further tragedies. Prior to the recent expansion of HCMC's administrative boundaries to include Binh Duong and Vung Tau, official statistics recorded more than 200,000 trees lining over 1,200 city roads. Roughly 7,600 of these trees stand 20 to 50 meters tall, primarily concentrated in central districts. Many are decades-old dipterocarp and Hopea trees, distinguished by their large trunks and heavy branches, which pose a significant risk of breaking or uprooting during severe weather. An Duong Vuong Street is heavily shaded by these towering old-growth dipterocarps, known for their straight trunks and dense, year-round green foliage. However, the thoroughfare has a deadly track record regarding falling debris. In September 2024, a 20-cm-thick dipterocarp branch fell from nearly 20 m near the same university, killing a 52-year-old woman. Eight years earlier, in 2016, a dipterocarp measuring over 30 m tall and a meter in diameter was uprooted during heavy rain on the street, crushing a 25-year-old man who later died from his injuries.

The third most visited country in Southeast Asia after Malaysia and Thailand welcomed nearly 16 million international visitors in the first eight months of 2026, up 14.4% year-on-year, driving up demand across hotels, travel companies, transport, restaurants and tourist attractions. A 2026 survey by Hoteljob.vn found that nearly 90% of tourism businesses planned to recruit. In Ho Chi Minh City alone, 89.7% of businesses were hiring, while 71.8% said recruitment was difficult or very difficult. The biggest shortages were among frontline workers, particularly in housekeeping, engineering, food service, front-office operations, and kitchens. The Politburo's Resolution dated Aug. 22, along with the government's action programme adopted on Sept. 7, set the target for tourism to directly contribute 10-12% of GDP by 2030, attracting 45-50 million international visitors and generate total revenue of US$80-90 billion. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Da Nang are envisioned as major tourism growth hubs, while Phu Quoc emerges as a new hub. These targets will place greater demands on the tourism workforce, not only in terms of numbers but also skills, from frontline workers and foreign-language guides to managers, technology specialists and professionals delivering high-end services. Ho Chi Minh City's tourism sector, for example, is facing gaps in supervisory and management positions, as businesses seek staff capable of operating in an increasingly digitalized, international and competitive environment. Foreign-language tour guides are another weak link. Demand is rising rapidly from markets such as Russia and India, while arrivals from Europe and the Middle East are also increasing. Yet training guides with the language skills and cultural knowledge needed to serve these markets can take years. The labor crunch is even more acute in destinations far from major urban centers. In Con Dao, hotels and resorts regularly struggle to recruit receptionists, housekeepers, chefs, and service staff, while travel companies face shortages of sales, marketing, and tour guide staff. Higher salaries have done little to solve the problem. The island's high cost of living and distance from the mainland make it difficult to attract and retain skilled workers, with many leaving after only a few months. According to Hoteljob.vn, 79.5% of tourism businesses have raised salaries or improved benefits over the past year. Yet 59.2% cited lower incomes compared with other industries as a key reason young people leave the profession, while limited career prospects were another major factor. Experts say Vietnam's tourism labor shortage is not simply about training more people. The bigger challenge is narrowing the gap between what schools teach and what employers need. Nearly 80% of businesses surveyed said fewer than 20% of young applicants could start work immediately, while more than 84% said new recruits needed at least a month before they could work independently. Employers are also increasingly concerned with workplace discipline, service mindset and the ability to work under pressure, rather than technical skills alone. Experts say stronger links with policymakers, training institutions and businesses are needed to better forecast demand, redesign training and give young workers clearer career paths. Vietnam's tourism goals will require a workforce to match. If training and retention continue to lag behind visitor growth, the industry's labor shortage could become one of its biggest bottlenecks on the road to 2030.

picked.t: Patients pack Ho Chi Minh City's largest hospital from dawn as daily visits top 10,000
picked.body: Patients wait to see doctors at Cho Ray Hospital on Sept. 15. Reception counters at the hospital, the largest in southern Vietnam, begin issuing queue numbers at 4:30 a.m., leaving waiting halls packed before doctors started consultations at 6 a.m. Patient volumes at the hospital have jumped sharply since the beginning of this month. Dr. Le Trung Nhan, head of the Outpatient Department, said the facility typically receives 8,000 to 9,000 patient visits per day, with figures exceeding 10,000 on some days such as Sept. 7. Automatic ticket kiosks and reception counters remain heavily frequented, though conditions have eased over the past year following the introduction of an app-based appointment registration system that cuts down on early morning queues. More than 70% of patients now schedule visits in advance via the app, requiring them only to print their queue numbers upon arrival before heading straight to consultation rooms. To help manage the flow, personnel from the hospital's Social Work Department and a team of volunteers, primarily university students, deploy early each morning to guide and support arriving patients. The hospital experiences its heaviest congestion between 7 and 8 a.m., when nearly every walkway becomes jammed with arriving patients and family members. Security personnel and volunteers are stationed throughout the halls, continuously instructing crowds to keep to the side to preserve clear pathways for wheelchairs and priority medical cases. After clearing reception counters, patients move into the payment section, where rows of waiting chairs quickly fill to capacity. An exhausted patient falls asleep in a crowded waiting hall. Statistics reveal that visitors from other provinces and municipalities make up more than 90% of all visits to the Outpatient Department. This sustained influx is largely fueled by individuals requiring routine check-ups for chronic illnesses, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and organ transplants. Overall, follow-up examinations account for roughly 60% of all patient traffic. With seating rows completely filled, 65-year-old Thu leaned against a pillar waiting for her turn outside the examination room after an early morning arrival. She reached the hospital at 5 a.m. following a more than four-hour bus journey from Bao Loc in Lam Dong Province near Da Lat, to HCMC. Thu had been experiencing persistent headaches, lightheadedness, dizziness, and numbness in both legs for several months. When local treatment in her hometown yielded no improvement after more than a month, she decided to seek medical attention at Cho Ray, where physicians ordered blood tests, an ultrasound, and a CT scan. Reflecting on changes at the facility, she noted that previous visits years ago involved long, exhausting lines simply to secure a queue number.
